To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
there is an association between the regional variation in cancer and industrial and air pollution exposure, and that the effect is not limited to the respiratory tract.

the regional distribution of mortality from cancer of all sites and of the respiratory system and heart diseases is significantly associated with the distribution of the concentration of air pollutants and industrial emissions in the Houston metropolitan area.
the mortality rate from cancer of the lung in the white non-Hispanic group is significantly higher in the regions of Houston that have a higher concentration of air and industrial pollutants.

the effects of air pollutants and industrial carcinogens in the environment on the human population in the Houston area.

there is a significant association between air pollution in Houston and cancer of the respiratory system and heart disease.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cancer is a complex disease and that its cause is multifactorial.

the industrial and environmental influence in Houston, as reflected by the mortality data of the 30-year period studied, has had a significant effect in increasing the regional mortality from cancer and other diseases and conditions.
the environmental carcinogen problem in the city of Houston is a real one, but it is not a simple one.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a need for the industrial and scientific communities to work together to explore the carcinogenic potential and other health hazards of the microchemical environmental pollutants.
there is a strong need to continue to investigate the effects of environmental pollution on cancer incidence and to explore the potential of microchemical pollutants as a cause of human cancer.
